```{ojs}
  marginBottom: 46,
  ariaLabel: "Cumulative gain curves: negatives found against corpus read, one line per representation",
  x: { label: "% of the corpus read", domain: [0, 100], grid: true },
  y: { label: "% of all negative reviews found", domain: [0, 100], grid: true },
  color: { legend: true, domain: ["lsa", "minilm", "e5"],
           range: [figColor("navy"), figColor("accent"), figColor("rose")] },
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 100, y: 100}],
      { x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3" }),
    Plot.text([{x: 72, y: 63}], { x: "x", y: "y", text: ["reading at random"],
      fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.65, fontSize: 12, rotate: -32 }),
    Plot.line(triageRows, { x: "read", y: "found", stroke: "rep", strokeWidth: 2 }),
    Plot.dot(triageRows, { x: "read", y: "found", fill: "rep", r: 3.5,
      title: d => `${d.rep}\nread ${d.read}% → found ${d.found}%` })
  ]
})
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The left-hand end is the only part that matters, because that is where a fixed
reading budget sits. E5 buys 56% of the complaints for 13% of the reading; LSA
needs 35.6% of the corpus for the same recall.
:::
::::

::: {.column-margin}
The dashed diagonal is what reading in random order gets you: read 40% of the
corpus, find 40% of the complaints. Every curve above it is value the clustering
created.
:::

The single number to take away:

> Reading **13.3%** of the corpus — the one E5 cluster with the worst positive
> rate — surfaces **56.0%** of every negative review in it.

That is a 4.2× improvement in the return on a fixed reading budget, from a
clustering that never saw a label. If your actual job is "find the complaints
so we can fix the product", this clustering did the job, and the ARI of 0.0075
that it scored on the way is irrelevant to that job.

Read that as a descriptive result, not as a validated policy. The *clusters*
are unsupervised, but the **order** they are read in is not: the ten clusters
were sorted by the negative rate computed from all 49,849 gold labels, and then
the recall was measured against those same labels. That is an oracle ordering
scored on its own answer key, and it tells you the clusters are separable
enough to be worth ranking — not how well a ranking you could actually build
would do. The deployable version costs a few hundred labels: rank the clusters
on a small labelled development sample, then measure recall on a disjoint test
sample. Exercise 8 is that experiment, and the gap between it and this number
is the honest cost of the shortcut taken here.

The ranking mostly holds along the whole curve, not just at the first point.
MiniLM is above LSA at every budget, and E5 is above both over the entire range
that anyone would actually operate in. LSA has to read **35.6%** of the corpus
to reach the recall E5 reaches at 13.3% — two and a half times the reading for
the same result.

The honest caveat is in the tail: between roughly 76% and 85% read, MiniLM
creeps above E5 by about 0.1 percentage points of recall. That is a real
crossing in the data and not worth a decision, because by then both have found
97% of the negatives and you are choosing between reading three-quarters of the
corpus and reading four-fifths of it. Triage curves are for the left-hand end.

### What the cluster actually contains

Metrics are cheap; read the documents. Five negative reviews drawn at random
from E5's worst cluster, with translations:

``` text
ürün paslandı. almanızı tavsiye etmem
  "The product rusted. I would not recommend buying it."

hiçbir işe yaramıyor. hatta dahada kötü hale getiriyor. kesinlikle alınmaz.
  "It does nothing. It actually makes things worse. Absolutely do not buy."

ürün çok çabuk ısınıyor ve çok yavaş
  "The product overheats very quickly and is very slow."

kalitesiz, arka plaka fotoğraftaki gibi tek parça değil, montajı zor.
  "Poor quality, the back plate is not one piece like in the photo,
   hard to assemble."

hiç beklediğim gibi değildi, yorumlardaki tüm olumsuzluklar aynen çıktı.
  "Not at all what I expected; every negative thing in the reviews
   turned out to be true."
```

These are not subtle. They are the reviews a product manager needs on Monday
morning, and the clustering put a disproportionate share of them in one bucket
without being told that "complaint" is a category.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The transferable lesson.** Before you report that a clustering "failed",
write down the decision the clustering was supposed to support and measure
*that*. Purity, ARI and NMI answer "did you recover my labels". Lift, recall at
a budget, and time-to-first-insight answer "did you help". They are different
questions and they can have opposite answers on the same run.
:::

## Naming clusters with a language model {#sec-naming-clusters}

c-TF-IDF gives you ten words. A stakeholder wants a phrase. This is the one
place in the pipeline where an LLM is unambiguously the right tool, and it is
worth being precise about why: naming is a *low-stakes, high-volume, verifiable*
task. Ten labels, each checkable in thirty seconds against the documents. This
is now a documented pattern rather than a trick — @pham2024topicgpt evaluates
prompt-driven topic labelling end to end against LDA and BERTopic and finds the
labels markedly more usable while the underlying grouping quality is unchanged,
which is exactly the division of labour to expect: the embedding groups, the
language model describes.

The pattern is the same one from @sec-prompting — give it the evidence, not the
task description alone:

``` text
Below are the 10 most distinctive words for a cluster of Turkish product
reviews, and 8 reviews sampled from it.

Distinctive words: koku, kokusu, parfüm, kalıcı, güzel, tavsiye, parfümü,
aldım, ederim, var

Reviews:
1. ...
2. ...

Give a 2-5 word English label naming what this cluster is about. If the
reviews do not share a coherent subject, answer exactly: NO COHERENT THEME.
```

Three details make the difference between this being useful and being a
liability:

1. **Sample the documents, do not only pass the words.** The words are already
   a lossy summary; an LLM given only `bi ye fi tavsi çi` will confabulate a
   theme for it, which is precisely the failure @sec-dotted-i is about.
2. **Give it an escape hatch.** The `NO COHERENT THEME` option is what turns
   the model from a label generator into a weak detector of junk clusters. A
   cluster the model refuses to name is a cluster you should look at yourself.
3. **Sample from the whole cluster, not just near the centroid.** Centroid
   documents are the most typical, so a centroid-only sample makes every cluster
   look tidier than it is, and hides exactly the heterogeneity you want to know
   about before you name it.

**The one number this section owes you, and does not have.** Rule 2 is a claim
about a detector, and this chapter's own rule is that you do not trust a
detector until you have measured it (@sec-dotted-i is the cautionary tale). The
test is sitting right here and costs eleven prompts: run this template on all
ten E5 clusters *and* on LSA cluster 7 — the ten tokenizer fragments with no
meaning at all — and record how many E5 labels survive a 20-document spot check,
how often `NO COHERENT THEME` fires, and whether it fires on LSA 7. We have not
run it, so treat rule 2 as a design principle rather than a measured safeguard.
That last cell is the one worth carrying into your own pipeline: **an escape
hatch that never fires is not a detector, it is decoration.**

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A generated label is a hypothesis, not a finding.** The model has seen ten
words and eight documents out of five thousand. It will produce a fluent,
plausible name for a cluster that is actually three unrelated things stuck
together, because producing fluent plausible names is what it does. Spot-check
every label against 20 documents you sampled yourself before any of them reaches
a slide.
:::

## Intuition checks {#sec-clustering-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument, so the answers carry numbers you
can check.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Two documents score a cosine of 0.91. Are they near-duplicates?

Nobody can tell you yet, including you, until the random-pair background is on
the table. Under tf-idf two *unrelated* reviews in this corpus average 0.0182
and the 99th percentile of 4.5 million random pairs is 0.1300 — so 0.91 is far
off the end of the scale and "near-duplicate" is the right reading. Under E5 the
same corpus has a random-pair mean of **0.8547** with a standard deviation of
0.0278 and a 99th percentile of 0.9155. There, 0.91 sits about two standard
deviations above the mean of documents that have nothing to do with each other,
and a duplicate detector thresholded at 0.90 would flag a large fraction of
every pair in the corpus.

Same number, opposite conclusions. The only thing separating them is four lines
of code, run once, before you look at a single similarity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your silhouette never exceeds 0.10 and your ARI is zero. Did the clustering fail?

Those two numbers say the partition is not well separated and is not the label
partition. Neither of them says it is worthless, and treating them as if they
did is the most common way people talk themselves out of a usable result.

The same $k=10$ E5 clustering that scored ARI **+0.0075** has a cluster that is
26.8% negative against a 6.34% base rate — a **4.23× lift** — and reading 13.3%
of the corpus in oracle cluster order finds 56.0% of its complaints. The clustering did
not change between those two sentences; the question did.

So the honest diagnosis is rarely "the clustering failed". It is "I scored it
against a question nobody was asking". Write down the decision the clustering
was supposed to support, measure *that*, and only then decide.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why deduplicate before clustering rather than after?

Because k-means moves each centre to the **mean** of its members, so sixty
copies of one sentence cast sixty votes on where that centre lands. A duplicate
group is a weight, not a row. The same argument applies to every idf you fit and
every topic model you run downstream.

The second reason is that the count is a free diagnostic of your collection
pipeline. Ours came back at 151 redundant documents at $J \geq 0.8$, in 27
seconds, without performing any meaningful share of the $1.25 \times 10^9$
pairwise comparisons. Had it come back at 20% you would have stopped and gone to
read the scraper, and that would have been a better use of the afternoon than
any clustering.

One caveat to state whenever you report the number: it is a lower bound. At
`threshold=0.8`, `datasketch` bands the 128 hashes so that a pair sitting
*exactly* at 0.8 is examined with probability 0.40. "At least 151", never
"exactly 151".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. HDBSCAN calls 97% of your corpus noise. A colleague proposes running UMAP to five dimensions first, "because then it finds clusters." What do you say?

That the sentence is true and that it is not evidence. UMAP optimises a
low-dimensional layout to preserve a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph, and squeezing
a corpus into five dimensions manufactures density contrast whether or not the
original space had any. Clusters appearing after UMAP is the expected outcome of
running UMAP, not a discovery about your data.

What would turn it into a finding is a check UMAP never saw: do the groups
predict something held out, do they survive a change of `n_neighbors` and
`random_state`, do they survive on a random half of the corpus. Our own evidence
points the other way — E5's random-pair cosine is 0.8547 with a standard
deviation of 0.0278, so every document sits at nearly the same distance from
every other, and a space that uniform has no density variation to be revealed.

None of which forbids shipping the UMAP pipeline. Ship it on the strength of the
downstream number, not on the strength of the picture.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your best topic scores three times the coherence of the next best. What do you do first?

Read it. Ours was `bi ye fi tavsi çi ederi si ni li yi` — ten tokenizer
fragments, all manufactured by the same Unicode defect in the same documents,
which is precisely why they co-occur almost perfectly and why NPMI scored them
**+0.5075**, the highest per-topic coherence anywhere in the chapter. Coherence
rewards co-occurrence, and a systematic bug is the most reliable co-occurrence
in any corpus.

The damage was not confined to that one topic either. Dropping it takes LSA's
mean from +0.1340 to +0.0925 — from first place to last among the three c-TF-IDF
rows. One topic in ten, of a kind a human rejects in two seconds, was carrying
the ranking. @chang2009reading published the general form of this result in
2009; this is just our own numbers agreeing with it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. You could label 500 documents and train a classifier. When is clustering still the right tool?

When you do not yet know what the classes are. That is the core of it: a
classifier needs a label set, and clustering is one of the few honest ways to
discover what that set should be. "Run k-means, read 20 documents per cluster,
draft the guidelines from what you read" is a real and cheap way to open an
annotation project — @sec-data-annotation is the chapter that then tells you how
to check the guidelines hold up.

Three other cases: you have far more documents than anyone will ever read and
must choose which to read (@sec-clustering-payoff); you must describe a corpus to
somebody who will not read it either (@sec-topic-models); or you want to know
what is actually in your data, including the parts nobody put there on purpose
(@sec-dotted-i).

And the converse, which matters just as much: if you already know the classes
and can afford to label, label. Clustering is not a cheaper classifier and it
will not become one.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-clustering-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On attribution — the same caution as @sec-text-as-data.** These are questions
that recur across the two credible public sources, both free:
[*Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews*](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/)
by Chip Huyen [@huyen2021interviews] and
[Machine Learning Interviews](https://github.com/alirezadir/Machine-Learning-Interviews).
Treat any page claiming to list "the questions company X asks" as marketing.
:::

1. **How do you choose the number of clusters?** The answer interviewers are
   listening for begins by refusing the premise. Internal indices disagree —
   ours put the optimum at 50, 2 and 50 on one representation and 2, 2 and 4 on
   another — and in two of three cases the "optimum" was a 1–7% wobble on a flat
   line. Say what you would do instead: cluster at three or four values of $k$,
   read 20 documents per cluster, and keep the $k$ whose clusters you can each
   describe in one line. Then mention the elbow method only to say you do not
   use it, and why — optimal inertia falls monotonically by construction, which
   guarantees nothing about a usable bend, and where you read one depends on your
   axis limits [@schubert2023stop].

2. **k-means or HDBSCAN?** k-means assumes spherical clusters of similar extent,
   no outliers, and a known $k$; on text it is assumptions 2 and 3 that hurt, not
   the one everybody names. HDBSCAN drops all four and adds a noise class, which
   is the right shape for a corpus where most documents belong to nothing in
   particular. The catch is that it can decline to answer, and on this corpus it
   did: 53–100% noise depending on `min_cluster_size`, never more than three
   clusters at any setting, and where it kept most of the documents it kept them
   in a single lump holding 47% of everything. A strong answer says "run both,
   because they disagree in informative ways" — two methods with different
   assumptions both reporting no structure is much stronger evidence than either
   alone.

3. **Why cosine and not Euclidean on text?** Because raw length carries document
   length rather than topic, and you almost never want to cluster by length. The
   part worth knowing beyond that: on $\ell_2$-normalised vectors the two are
   monotonically related, $d^2 = 2 - 2\cos$, so they induce the same nearest
   neighbours — but *not* the same k-means, because the arithmetic mean of unit
   vectors is not a unit vector, so from the second iteration the two procedures
   diverge. The practical rule is to normalise, then keep the metric consistent
   between the algorithm and every score you report. A silhouette computed with
   Euclidean distance on a clustering fitted with cosine is not measuring your
   clustering.

4. **Find the near-duplicates in a billion documents.** Shingle, MinHash, band,
   bucket, verify — and then say what the approximation actually costs, which is
   where most answers stop short. LSH produces no false positives that survive
   exact verification, but it does produce false negatives: with 128 hashes in 9
   bands of 13 at a 0.8 threshold, a pair at $J = 0.9$ is examined with
   probability 0.93, one at $J = 0.8$ with probability 0.40, and one at $J = 0.7$
   with probability 0.08. That is the deliberate design point, not a defect, and
   it is why duplicate counts are reported as lower bounds. Mention SimHash
   [@charikar2002similarity] as the alternative when you need to check new
   documents against a standing index rather than audit a fixed corpus.

5. **How do you evaluate a clustering when you have no labels?** Start with the
   internal indices and their limits, then get to the real answer: evaluate the
   decision, not the partition. Sample and read; check that a human can name each
   cluster; and where a downstream use exists, measure it directly. Our own
   numbers are the argument — ARI could not separate three representations, all
   ≈ 0, while lift in the worst cluster ranked them 1.67× / 2.79× / 4.23× from
   the identical assignments. If you have any labelled subset at all, however
   small, it buys you more than every internal index combined.

6. **LDA, or something newer?** State the assumption that decides it: LDA is a
   bag-of-words mixture model that needs enough words per document to estimate a
   mixture from. On our 19-word median reviews it was **133× slower than NMF and
   less coherent** (+0.0737 against +0.1183). For short text, NMF on tf-idf is
   the better classical default, and the modern default is cluster-then-describe
   — embed, cluster, and label with c-TF-IDF [@grootendorst2022bertopic], which
   costs nothing once the clustering exists. The trade to name out loud: c-TF-IDF
   inherits all of the embedding's semantics and all of the clustering's
   mistakes, and it is a labelling procedure rather than a topic model. LDA is
   still the right answer when documents are long and you genuinely need a
   per-document mixture rather than an assignment.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-clustering-tools}

Everything in this chapter ran on one laptop with the versions below. Pinning
versions in a book is a hostage to fortune, but not pinning them is worse — the
numbers here are only reproducible against a stated stack.

| library | version used | what it is for here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `scikit-learn` | 1.9.0 | `TfidfVectorizer`, `TruncatedSVD`, `KMeans`, `HDBSCAN`, `LatentDirichletAllocation`, `NMF`, and every metric |
| `sentence-transformers` | 5.7.0 | loading and batching MiniLM and E5 |
| `torch` | 2.13.0 | the MPS backend the embeddings ran on |
| `numpy` / `scipy` | 2.5.2 / 1.18.0 | dense and sparse linear algebra |
| `pandas` | 3.0.5 | corpus handling, Parquet round-trip |
| `datasketch` | 2.0.0 | MinHash and the LSH index for @sec-near-dupes |
| `umap-learn` | 0.5.12 | the projection discussed in @sec-density |

: The stack these numbers came from. Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon
{tbl-colwidths="[26,16,58]"}

**Versions are half of reproducibility; hyperparameters are the other half, and
this chapter under-reports them.** Three gaps to close before you rerun any of
this. `KMeans` is randomised through k-means++, so its `random_state` and
`n_init` decide the partition — and `n_init` has defaulted to `"auto"` since
scikit-learn 1.4, which means the default itself is version-dependent. `HDBSCAN`
has `min_samples`, `metric`, `cluster_selection_method` and
`cluster_selection_epsilon` beside the `min_cluster_size` we swept
(@sec-density). `LatentDirichletAllocation` has `learning_method`, `max_iter`
and the two Dirichlet priors. Fix all of them explicitly in your own runs and
print them beside the numbers — including the ones you did not change, because
"we used the default" is only a statement if you say which version's default.

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `bertopic` | 0.17.4 | the whole embed → UMAP → HDBSCAN → c-TF-IDF pipeline as one object, with topic merging, hierarchies and LLM naming built in. The fastest way to a demo; read @sec-density before trusting the clusters |
| `faiss-cpu` | 1.15.0 | approximate nearest neighbours when the corpus stops fitting in a dense similarity matrix — roughly past a million documents |
| `usearch` | 2.26.0 | a lighter, newer alternative to FAISS with the same job |
| `gensim` | 4.4.0 | the classical topic-model toolkit; still the reference implementation for LDA variants and `CoherenceModel` |
| `top2vec` | 1.0.36 | joint document/word embeddings with automatic topic count; conceptually close to BERTopic and predates it |
| `chromadb` | 1.5.9 | when the vectors need to persist and be queried by an application rather than a script — the bridge to @sec-rag |

: The wider ecosystem, versions as of writing {tbl-colwidths="[16,14,70]"}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Choosing, in one line each.** Under ~100k documents, scikit-learn does
everything in this chapter and you should write the twenty lines yourself so you
can see what each step did. Over that, add FAISS or `usearch` for the
neighbour search. Reach for BERTopic when you want the polished artefact rather
than the understanding — and having read @sec-dotted-i, you now know which of
its defaults to distrust.
:::

## Lab: build a triage curve for a corpus you own {#sec-clustering-lab}

The deliverable is one sentence of the form *"reading X% of the corpus finds Y%
of the Z"*, plus the curve that justifies it. That sentence is what makes
clustering fundable, and it is worth far more than a silhouette score.

### What you need

Any corpus of a few thousand short documents in a domain you understand —
support tickets, survey free-text, issue titles, exam answers. It needs one
binary property you care about (complaint / not, urgent / not, off-topic / not)
that you can label on a *sample*, not on all of it. Labelling 300 documents is
enough and is the whole point: the lab simulates having a small budget.

`scikit-learn` and `sentence-transformers` do everything. The E5 pass on 50k
documents took 104 seconds on a laptop GPU (Apple Silicon, `mps`); on CPU
expect roughly an order of magnitude more, so budget a few minutes for 5k
documents and start it before you read the rest of this section.

### Step 1 — deduplicate first, and count what you removed

Run MinHash + LSH at $J \geq 0.8$ before anything else, exactly as in
@sec-near-dupes. Report the number of groups and the largest group. If more than
about 5% of your corpus is near-duplicate, stop and find out why — you have
probably discovered a data-collection bug, and that is already a result worth
reporting.

### Step 2 — embed twice, deliberately

Build both a tf-idf → SVD(256) representation and a sentence-embedding one.
Two representations is the minimum that lets you say anything comparative, and
the comparison is the interesting part. Before clustering, compute the
**random-pair background**: sample 2,000 documents, take all pairwise cosines,
and record the mean and standard deviation for each space. You will need these
to interpret every similarity you look at afterwards, and computing them takes
four lines.

### Step 3 — sweep $k$, and expect to be disappointed

Run k-means at $k \in \{2, 5, 10, 20, 50\}$ on both representations. Record
silhouette (on a fixed sample if the corpus is large), the size of the largest
cluster, and the fit time. Plot silhouette against $k$.

If your curve is flat and low, you have reproduced our result and you should
**not** conclude that you did it wrong. Note the largest-cluster column: a
"clustering" whose biggest group holds 60% of the corpus is one lump and a
scattering, whatever $k$ you asked for.

### Step 4 — label 300 documents, stratified by cluster

This is the step people skip. At your chosen $k$, sample **30 documents from
each of 10 clusters** rather than 300 at random, and label your binary property
by hand. Stratifying is what makes the next step possible at this budget:
a random sample of 300 would put only a handful of documents in your rarest
cluster and give you a per-cluster rate you cannot trust.

Write down the per-cluster positive rate and a 95% interval for each. At $n=30$
those intervals are wide — roughly $\pm 17$ points near 50% — so treat them as
"is this cluster different from the corpus at all?" rather than as point
estimates.

### Step 5 — the curve, and the sentence

Sort the clusters by their measured rate, worst first. Walk down the list
accumulating the share of the corpus read against the share of your property
found, using the cluster sizes you know exactly and the rates you estimated.
Plot it against the diagonal, as in @sec-clustering-payoff.

Then write the sentence. If your curve lies on the diagonal, the honest sentence
is *"clustering does not help triage this property in this corpus"* — which is a
finding, cost you an afternoon, and has saved you from building a pipeline on it.

### Going further

- **Rerun step 5 with the other representation.** Our two differed by 2.5× in
  lift while being indistinguishable under ARI. Yours may too, and if so you
  have just chosen your embedding model on evidence.
- **Run the Unicode check from @sec-dotted-i on your own text**, whatever
  language it is in: assert that lowercasing then tokenising is idempotent, that `İSTANBUL` lowercases to `istanbul` and `IŞIK` to `ışık`, and count the vocabulary types that vanish when you normalise properly.
- **Name your clusters with an LLM using the recipe in @sec-naming-clusters**,
  then check every label against 20 documents you sampled yourself. Count how
  many labels survive. That ratio is your calibration for trusting the next
  batch.

## Exercises {#sec-clustering-exercises}

1. **The metric that was measuring nothing.** In @sec-kmeans the best adjusted
   Rand index anywhere in the sweep was 0.0083, and in @sec-clustering-payoff
   the same clusterings separated cleanly at 1.67×, 2.79× and 4.23×. Both
   numbers are correct. Explain, in terms of what ARI counts, how a partition
   can carry that much decision-relevant signal and still score zero. Then
   construct a small worked example — ten documents, two labels, two clusters —
   where ARI is exactly 0 and the lift in one cluster is 2×.

2. **A background you have not computed.** A colleague reports that two
   documents in their corpus have a cosine similarity of 0.91 under E5 and
   concludes they are near-duplicates. Using the numbers in
   @sec-what-similar-means, say what is wrong with the inference, what single
   quantity they should compute before making it, and what value of that
   quantity would make their conclusion reasonable.

3. **The tokenizer test you do not have.** @sec-dotted-i found a defect that
   survives exact deduplication and both NFC and NFKC normalisation.
   @sec-bake-off avoided it only because a Turkish speaker knew to write
   `tr_lower`. (a) Explain why a classifier trained and tested on the *same*
   defective pipeline shows no accuracy loss. (b) Name the deployment change
   that would suddenly make it visible. (c) Write the three-line property test
   you would add to a CI suite to catch this class of bug in a language you do
   not speak — noting that `assert tokenize(s.upper()) == tokenize(s)` is the
   wrong answer, and saying why.

4. **Density, honestly.** HDBSCAN called 97% of the corpus noise on LSA and
   99.5% on E5. A teammate proposes running UMAP to 5 dimensions first, "because
   then it finds clusters". (a) Explain what UMAP changes about the input that
   makes clusters appear. (b) Design an experiment that would distinguish
   "UMAP revealed structure that was there" from "UMAP created structure that
   was not". (c) Say which result would make you willing to ship the UMAP
   pipeline anyway.

5. **The coherence trap, in your own data.** Take the highest-coherence topic
   from any topic model you have run and read 20 documents that scored highest
   on it. If the topic is real, write the one-line description a colleague could
   use to sort new documents into it. If it is not, identify what the model
   actually latched onto. Report which happened — and note that in this chapter
   the highest-coherence topic in the entire run was the second case.

6. **The claim in a footnote that we did not measure.** `[^normeq]` says
   Euclidean k-means on $\ell_2$-normalised vectors and spherical k-means
   "usually land in similar places on text", and admits that is folklore. Settle
   it. Write spherical k-means — Lloyd's algorithm with the centroids
   re-normalised to unit length after every update — run both at $k=10$ on the
   same vectors, and report the ARI between the two partitions for each
   representation. Then check whether the worst-cluster lift in
   @sec-clustering-payoff moves. Say which of the two results would make you
   change the footnote, and how.

7. **Choosing $k$ without an index.** You have 40,000 support tickets and a
   support team of six people who will each own one category. Argue for a value
   of $k$ using no internal validation index at all. State what would make you
   revise it, and explain why this reasoning is *better* founded than an elbow
   plot rather than merely more convenient.
8. **Turn the triage result into a policy you could deploy.** @sec-clustering-payoff
   ranks the ten clusters by a negative rate computed from every gold label, then
   scores recall against those same labels. Redo it honestly: hold out a random
   test half, label a development sample of 300 documents from the other half,
   rank the clusters by the negative rate *in that sample only*, and then read
   the triage curve on the test half. Report how much of the 56.0%-at-13.3%
   result survives, and how the answer moves as you shrink the development
   sample to 100 and grow it to 1,000.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-clustering-deeper}

Before any paper: run your clustering twice with different seeds and compare
the assignments. If they disagree, every interpretation you were about to
write is about the seed.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [BERTopic documentation](https://maartengr.github.io/BERTopic/) | unusually good docs — the "best practices" page is a short course in what goes wrong |
| [UMAP documentation](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) | includes an honest page on how to *misread* UMAP plots, which is the most common failure in this chapter's territory |
| [scikit-learn clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html) | the algorithms side by side, with the assumptions each one makes stated plainly |
| [`hdbscan`](https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan) | read the noise-handling section; it explains why so much of your corpus comes back unlabelled |
| [Sentence Transformers](https://sbert.net/) | the embeddings everything here is built on, with a clear guide to picking one |
| [Visualizing High-Dimensional Space](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wvsE8jm1GzE) — Google | four minutes on what a projection does and does not preserve; watch it before trusting any UMAP plot |

## What to remember {#sec-clustering-summary}

- **Clustering is what you do when you cannot read the corpus and do not have
  labels.** It is not a weaker form of classification; it answers a different
  question, and the metrics that judge classifiers judge it badly.
- **Similarity is a property of the geometry, not of the documents.** A cosine
  of 0.98 means nothing until you know what two random documents score. In our
  four spaces the random-pair mean ranged from 0.018 to 0.855, so the same
  number means "near-duplicate" in one space and "unremarkable" in another.
  Always compute the background.
- **Deduplicate before you do anything else.** It is cheap, it is the highest
  return per line of code in the chapter, and the count you get is a diagnostic
  of your collection pipeline. At $J \geq 0.8$ we removed 151 documents in 27
  seconds without comparing all 1.25 billion pairs.
- **k-means makes four assumptions on your behalf** — spherical clusters,
  similar extent, no outliers, and a known $k$ — and on text corpora it is
  numbers 2 and 3 that hurt, not the one everybody worries about.
- **A flat silhouette curve is a finding.** Ours never exceeded 0.1042 across
  42 runs, and HDBSCAN independently called 53–100% of the same corpus noise
  depending on `min_cluster_size`, never returning more than three clusters at
  any setting — and where it kept most of the documents it kept them in one
  lump holding half the corpus. Two methods with different assumptions agreeing
  that there are no boundaries is stronger evidence than either alone.
- **Do not use the elbow method.** A monotone curve is not a promise of a
  usable bend, where you read one depends on your axis limits, and
  @schubert2023stop sets out the case at length.
- **Short documents break LDA.** On 19-word reviews it was 133× slower than NMF
  and less coherent. If you have inherited an LDA pipeline on short text, run
  NMF beside it before defending the incumbent.
- **Cluster-then-describe is the modern default.** c-TF-IDF costs nothing once
  you have clusters, it inherits all of the embedding's semantics, and it
  inherits all of the clustering's mistakes.
- **Topic coherence can be maximised by garbage.** Our highest-scoring topic in
  the whole chapter, at +0.5075, was ten tokenizer fragments. Removing it moved
  its method from first place to last. @chang2009reading made this point in
  2009 and it has not stopped being true.
- **Unsupervised methods find what is actually in your data, including the parts
  you did not put there.** k-means assembled a cluster that was 94.7% affected
  by a Unicode defect against a 6.0% background, having been told nothing about
  Unicode. @sec-bake-off knew about that defect because a Turkish speaker did;
  the clustering found it without one.
- **`str.lower()` is not Turkish-aware, and NFKC will not save you.**
  `"TAVSİYE".lower()` tokenises to `['tavsi', 'ye']`. Pin the cases you care
  about — `assert tokenize("TAVSİYE") == tokenize("tavsiye")` — rather than
  asserting a general round-trip. `tokenize(s.upper()) == tokenize(s)` looks
  tidier and fails on correct code, because Python's `str.upper()` is not
  Turkish-aware either: it sends `i` to `I` instead of `İ`, so `iyi` comes back
  as `ıyı` no matter how good your lowercaser is.
- **Measure the decision, not the partition.** ARI could not distinguish our
  three representations; the triage curve ranked them cleanly and in the
  expected order. Under an ordering chosen from the full set of gold labels,
  reading 13.3% of the corpus found 56.0% of its complaints — a 4.2× return on a
  fixed budget from a clustering that scored zero on every external index. A
  policy you can deploy still needs that ordering chosen on one sample and
  measured on another.
- **"The clustering failed" is almost always premature.** Write down the
  decision it was supposed to support, measure that, and only then decide.
